title: Model Fitting Exercise
text:
Data cleaning

# keep only OCC == 1
mavo_occ1 <- mavo %>% filter(OCC == 1)

# split into the dosing rows (TIME == 0) and observation rows (TIME != 0)
dose_rows <- mavo_occ1 %>% filter(TIME == 0)
obs_rows  <- mavo_occ1 %>% filter(TIME != 0)

# total drug for each individual = sum of DV across observation rows
total_Y <- obs_rows %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarize(Y = sum(DV), .groups = "drop")

# get the baseline characteristics from the dosing row
baseline <- dose_rows %>%
  select(ID, DOSE, AGE, SEX, RACE, WT, HT)

# join total Y with baseline
mavo_clean <- baseline %>%
  inner_join(total_Y, by = "ID") %>%
  mutate(
    SEX = factor(SEX),
    RACE = factor(RACE)
  ) %>%
  select(Y, DOSE, AGE, SEX, RACE, WT, HT)

# Save the cleaned data as an RDS file for downstream exercises
saveRDS(mavo_clean, file = "mavo_clean.rds")

title: Project Part 1
text:
General Background Information
Microbiome research aims to characterize microbial communities and understand how they vary across environments or host conditions. Many microbiome studies rely on sequencing technologies such as 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, which generate high-dimensional count data that are often sparse and noisy. As a result, microbiome data analysis requires specialized workflows and tools that differ from standard analyses of simple rectangular datasets.
These data are commonly categorized as genetics or –omics data. While some –omics datasets can be represented in rectangular form, they typically have many more features than samples and require preprocessing steps such as filtering, normalization, and dimension reduction. The Bioconductor project provides a comprehensive collection of R packages and standardized data structures designed specifically for genetics and –omics data analysis, making it a natural framework for microbiome research.

title: Project Part 1
section: Description of data and data source
text:
Description of data and data source
The data used in this project are 16S rRNA sequencing data from the Human Microbiome Project (HMP), obtained using the HMP16SData Bioconductor package. The unit of observation is an individual microbiome sample. For each sample, the dataset contains a high-dimensional table of microbial feature counts, a taxonomy table assigning features to taxonomic ranks (e.g., phylum and genus), and sample-level metadata describing characteristics such as body site.
This dataset represents a complex data type because it is not a single rectangular data frame. Instead, it consists of multiple linked components that are stored in specialized data structures, such as SummarizedExperiment and phyloseq objects. The number of microbial features greatly exceeds the number of samples, and many features are rare or absent in most samples, motivating the use of filtering and transformation steps prior to modeling.

title: Project Part 1
text:
Questions/Hypotheses to be addressed
The primary question of this project is whether microbiome community structure differs across sample groups defined by available metadata, such as body site. Outcomes of interest include alpha diversity measures (e.g., Shannon diversity) that summarize within-sample diversity, as well as beta diversity measures that capture differences in community composition between samples. I hypothesize that samples from different body sites will exhibit distinct diversity patterns and will cluster separately in ordination analyses.

Data acquisition
The data were obtained directly from the Human Microbiome Project using the Bioconductor package HMP16SData. The V3–V5 16S rRNA amplicon dataset was imported programmatically in R using the V35() function, which returns the data as a SummarizedExperiment object containing microbial feature counts, taxonomic annotations, and sample metadata. The data were then converted to a phyloseq object to support microbiome-specific data handling and exploratory analysis. title: Project Part 1
text:
Exploratory/Descriptive analysis
Exploratory analyses were used to summarize key characteristics of the microbiome dataset and assess feasibility for later modeling. I first examined sequencing depth across samples to understand variability in read counts. Next, I summarized community composition by visualizing relative abundances of dominant taxonomic groups (phylum level). Finally, I computed alpha diversity (Shannon index) to describe within-sample diversity and compared it across a metadata-defined grouping variable (e.g., body subsite). These descriptive results provide a high-level overview of the data structure and major patterns without performing formal hypothesis testing. ### Sequencing depth distribution

tibble(library_size = sample_sums(ps_filt)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = library_size)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Sequencing depth (reads per sample)",
       y = "Number of samples")









Dominant taxa composition (top phyla)

# Extract relative abundance matrix
otu <- as(otu_table(ps_rel), "matrix")
if (taxa_are_rows(ps_rel)) otu <- t(otu)

# Get phylum labels
tax <- as(tax_table(ps_rel), "matrix")
phylum <- tax[, "PHYLUM"]
phylum[is.na(phylum) | phylum == ""] <- "UNASSIGNED"

# Collapse features to phylum level
otu_phylum <- rowsum(t(otu), group = phylum)
otu_phylum <- t(otu_phylum)

# Plot top 10 phyla
df <- as_tibble(otu_phylum, rownames = "SampleID") |>
  pivot_longer(-SampleID, names_to = "PHYLUM", values_to = "RelAbund")

  group_by(PHYLUM) |>
  summarize(total = sum(RelAbund), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(total, n = 10) |>
  pull(PHYLUM)

Hi everyone! My name is Kexin Cui (you can call me Cassie). I’m a second year Ph.D. student in Epidemiology and Biostatistics with a Data Analysis and Modelling (DAM) concentration, working in the Bahl Lab, and I have a background in Data Analytics. I’m taking EPID 8060E because it is a core requirement for my concentration.

Research Interests
My research interests focus on integrating machine learning models with statistical analysis to advance phylogenetic studies, with an emphasis on improving inference, interpretation, and visualization of evolutionary and transmission processes. I am particularly interested in infectious disease systems, where genomic data, ecological drivers, and surveillance data can be combined to better understand how pathogens spread across space and time.


Statistics, Modeling, and Programming Experience
I have experience with a range of statistical and modeling approaches, including:

Generalized linear models, including logistic, Poisson, quasi-Poisson, and negative binomial models
Survival analysis
Longitudinal data analysis
Network analysis and spatial modeling
Phylogenetic and phylodynamic modeling, including experience using BEAST to study evolutionary and transmission patterns

On the programming side, I primarily use R for data wrangling, statistical modeling, visualization, and reproducible reporting (e.g., tidyverse, ggplot2, Shiny, gtsummary). I also have experience using SAS for applied biostatistics coursework and Python for data processing and visualization. I am comfortable working with large, multi-source datasets and building reproducible analysis pipelines.


What I Hope to Learn in This Course
In this course, I hope to strengthen my ability to conduct end-to-end data analysis workflows, from formulating feasible research questions to selecting and justifying appropriate statistical and machine learning approaches. This is particularly relevant to my research in phylogenetic and phylodynamic studies, where modeling choices strongly influence inference and interpretation.
I am also interested in improving my skills in reproducible data processing and analysis, especially using R and GitHub, and in communicating complex results and uncertainty in a clear, interpretable way for diverse audiences.

Re-create the figure (static)
The original figure is a share-of-members-by-generation plot across Congresses. We compute the proportion of members in each generation for each Congress.

gen_levels <- c(
  "Gilded", "Progressive", "Missionary", "Lost", "Greatest", "Silent",

      generation == "baby boomer" ~ "Boomers",
      generation == "Generation X" ~ "Gen X",

      generation == "Generation Z" ~ "Gen Z",
      TRUE ~ generation

title: Model Fitting Exercise
text:
Model critique
Both Model 1 and Model 2 beat the null model on training, CV, and test RMSE, so both extract real signal from the predictors. Model 1 has limited practical utility because DOSE only takes three discrete values, so it can only output three predictions and cannot distinguish individuals at the same dose. Model 2 is a meaningful improvement: it has the lowest RMSE everywhere (train, CV, test), its predictions spread along the 45-degree line, and its bootstrap medians and 89% intervals are stable. Its main limitations are asymmetric residuals at the extremes (suggesting nonlinearity the linear model misses), a small sample (90 train / 30 test), and wider bootstrap intervals in the tails.

text:
Tuning without CV (apparent resampling)

# LASSO penalty grid
las_tune_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) %>% set_engine("glmnet")
las_wf <- workflow() %>% add_model(las_tune_spec) %>% add_formula(Y ~ .)
las_grid <- tibble(penalty = 10^seq(-5, 2, length.out = 50))

las_tune_apparent <- tune_grid(
  las_wf, resamples = apparent(mavo), grid = las_grid, metrics = metric_set(rmse)
)

# autoplot() doesn't work with apparent() (only one resample), so plot manually
collect_metrics(las_tune_apparent, summarize = FALSE) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = penalty, y = .estimate)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "LASSO tuning (apparent)", y = "RMSE") +
  theme_minimal()









# Random forest grid: tune mtry and min_n
rf_tune_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 300, mtry = tune(), min_n = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("ranger", seed = rngseed) %>%
  set_mode("regression")

rf_wf <- workflow() %>% add_model(rf_tune_spec) %>% add_formula(Y ~ .)
rf_grid <- grid_regular(mtry(range = c(1, 7)), min_n(range = c(1, 21)), levels = 7)

rf_tune_apparent <- tune_grid(
  rf_wf, resamples = apparent(mavo), grid = rf_grid, metrics = metric_set(rmse)
)

  ggplot(aes(x = mtry, y = .estimate, color = factor(min_n))) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Random forest tuning (apparent)", y = "RMSE", color = "min_n") +
  theme_minimal()








LASSO RMSE drops as the penalty shrinks (approaching OLS). RF RMSE drops with higher mtry and lower min_n — both signals are misleading because we are evaluating on training data.

lm_spec  <- linear_reg() %>% set_engine("lm")
las_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = 0.1, mixture = 1) %>% set_engine("glmnet")
rf_spec  <- rand_forest(trees = 300) %>%
  set_engine("ranger", seed = rngseed) %>%
  set_mode("regression")

# Fit on full data, all predictors
fit_lm  <- lm_spec  %>% fit(Y ~ ., data = mavo)
fit_las <- las_spec %>% fit(Y ~ ., data = mavo)
fit_rf  <- rf_spec  %>% fit(Y ~ ., data = mavo)

# Predictions and RMSE
pred_all <- bind_rows(
  tibble(model = "Linear", observed = mavo$Y, predicted = predict(fit_lm,  mavo)$.pred),
  tibble(model = "LASSO",  observed = mavo$Y, predicted = predict(fit_las, mavo)$.pred),
  tibble(model = "RF",     observed = mavo$Y, predicted = predict(fit_rf,  mavo)$.pred)
)

pred_all %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarize(rmse = sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2)))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  model   rmse
  <chr>  <dbl>
1 LASSO   572.
2 Linear  572.
3 RF      358.



ggplot(pred_all, aes(x = observed, y = predicted, color = model, shape = model)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(title = "Observed vs predicted (no tuning)", x = "Observed Y", y = "Predicted Y") +
  theme_minimal()








Linear and LASSO give nearly identical fits. RF fits much closer because it can capture nonlinearity and interactions.

title: Machine Learning Models Exercise
text:
Tuning without CV (apparent resampling)

# LASSO penalty grid
las_tune_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) %>% set_engine("glmnet")
las_wf <- workflow() %>% add_model(las_tune_spec) %>% add_formula(Y ~ .)
las_grid <- tibble(penalty = 10^seq(-5, 2, length.out = 50))

las_tune_apparent <- tune_grid(
  las_wf, resamples = apparent(mavo), grid = las_grid, metrics = metric_set(rmse)
)

# autoplot() doesn't work with apparent() (only one resample), so plot manually
collect_metrics(las_tune_apparent, summarize = FALSE) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = penalty, y = .estimate)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "LASSO tuning (apparent)", y = "RMSE") +
  theme_minimal()









# Random forest grid: tune mtry and min_n
rf_tune_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 300, mtry = tune(), min_n = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("ranger", seed = rngseed) %>%
  set_mode("regression")

rf_wf <- workflow() %>% add_model(rf_tune_spec) %>% add_formula(Y ~ .)
rf_grid <- grid_regular(mtry(range = c(1, 7)), min_n(range = c(1, 21)), levels = 7)

rf_tune_apparent <- tune_grid(
  rf_wf, resamples = apparent(mavo), grid = rf_grid, metrics = metric_set(rmse)
)

collect_metrics(rf_tune_apparent, summarize = FALSE) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mtry, y = .estimate, color = factor(min_n))) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Random forest tuning (apparent)", y = "RMSE", color = "min_n") +
  theme_minimal()








LASSO RMSE drops as the penalty shrinks (approaching OLS). RF RMSE drops with higher mtry and lower min_n — both signals are misleading because we are evaluating on training data.
